title: RAW UNREVIEWED: Benedict36: a food permission expires when the same sick recipient recovers
summary: RAW_UNREVIEWED_NOT_SELECTED_NOT_TESTED. The sick receive baths as needed and weak patients may eat flesh for recovery; when they improve they resume ordinary abstinence. The person persists while health status changes the permission. Permitted treatment and observed therapeutic success are different assertions.

source.work: Regula Benedicti in Ernest F. Henderson, Select Historical Documents, translation
source.span: Complete chapter36; contrast checked against chapter39 closing exception
source.layer: Historical primary work in an explicitly named translation; source content inspected, no medieval Voynich ownership implied

source_tradition: Monastic regulation and care of the sick
differentiating_relation: SICK/WEAK(PERSON) licenses FOOD_USE for an expressed purpose; IMPROVED_HEALTH(PERSON) closes that exception and reactivates ABSTAIN. The parallel bath rule varies permission frequency rather than making bathing universally forbidden to healthy people.
complete_source_account: The chapter requires care, an attendant and a separate place for sick community members while retaining duties of patients and superiors.
Bath access is conditioned on need and is less readily granted to healthy people, especially youths.
Flesh permission is linked to debility and restoration, then withdrawn when recipients improve; neglect remains the superior’s responsibility.
known_counterexplanation: A permanently privileged recipient-class reading leaves the permission after recovery. A therapeutic-success reading turns permission and purpose into proof that meat caused recovery. A healthy-bathing ban exaggerates a frequency restriction into absolute negation.
